offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first/second); Class 6 Felony (third within 10 years or fourth+)
penalty_max: 12 months (first/second); 5 years (third within 10 years or fourth+)
fine_max: $2,500 (first/second); $2,500 (third+, felony fine up to $2,500 unless otherwise specified)
elements: Defendant drove or operated a motor vehicle, engine, or train
While under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or a combination
BAC of 0.08 or higher, or impaired ability to operate safely
mandatory_minimum: $250 fine (first offense); $500 fine and 1 month jail (second within 5 years); $1,000 fine and 90 days jail (third within 10 years)
enhancements: BAC 0.15–0.20 (mandatory 5 additional days jail, first; 10 additional days, second)
BAC 0.20+ (mandatory 10 additional days jail, first; 20 additional days, second)
Third offense within 10 years (Class 6 Felony)
Fourth or subsequent offense (Class 6 Felony with mandatory minimum 1 year)
Passenger under 18 (additional mandatory 5 days; additional fine $500–$1,000)
notes: Virginia uses the term DWI (driving while intoxicated). Implied consent under Va. Code § 18.2-268.2. Refusal results in administrative license suspension. VASAP (Virginia Alcohol Safety Action Program) enrollment required for all convictions.

elements: Defendant drove or operated a motor vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or drugs or with BAC of 0.08 or higher
No prior DWI convictions within the lookback period
enhancements: BAC 0.15–0.20 (mandatory 5 days jail)
BAC 0.20+ (mandatory 10 days jail)
Minor passenger under 18 (additional mandatory 5 days jail)
notes: License revocation for 1 year. VASAP required. Restricted license available after completion of requirements.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (second); Class 6 Felony (third within 10 years or fourth+)
penalty_min: 20 days (second within 5 years); 10 days (second within 5–10 years); 90 days (third within 10 years); 1 year (fourth+)
elements: Defendant drove or operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated
One or more prior DWI convictions within the applicable lookback period
mandatory_minimum: $500 fine and 20 days jail (second within 5 years); $1,000 fine and 90 days jail (third within 10 years); 1 year (fourth or subsequent)
enhancements: Second within 5 years vs. 5–10 years (different mandatory minimums)
Third within 5 years (mandatory 6 months)
Fourth or subsequent (mandatory 1 year, Class 6 Felony)
notes: Three-year license revocation for second offense; indefinite revocation for third or subsequent. Ignition interlock required.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first); escalates same as alcohol DWI
elements: Defendant drove or operated a motor vehicle
While under the influence of any narcotic drug or self-administered intoxicant or drug
Or under the combined influence of alcohol and drugs
To a degree which impaired the defendant's ability to drive safely
enhancements: Same enhancement schedule as alcohol DWI for repeat offenses
notes: No per se limit for drugs; prosecution must prove impairment. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluations commonly used. Blood test required for drug cases.

statute_title: Refusal of Blood or Breath Test
offense_class: Civil violation (first refusal); Class 2 Misdemeanor (second refusal); Class 1 Misdemeanor (third+)
elements: Defendant was lawfully arrested for DWI
Defendant was informed of the implied consent law
Defendant unreasonably refused to submit to a blood or breath test
enhancements: Second refusal within 10 years (Class 2 Misdemeanor criminal charge)
Third or subsequent refusal within 10 years (Class 1 Misdemeanor)
notes: First offense refusal is a civil matter resulting only in license suspension. Second and subsequent are criminal. Refusal can be used as evidence at DWI trial.

elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a highway
At a speed of 20 mph or more in excess of the applicable maximum speed limit
Or at a speed in excess of 85 mph regardless of the speed limit
enhancements: Speed 90+ mph may result in license suspension
Reckless driving resulting in death is a Class 6 Felony under § 46.2-868
notes: Virginia is one of the few states where reckless driving is a criminal misdemeanor, not a traffic infraction. Commonly charged for speeds 80+ on highways. License suspension for 6 months possible.

statute_title: Driving on Suspended or Revoked License
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a Virginia highway
While defendant's license was suspended, revoked, or had been restricted
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (mandatory 10 days jail)
Driving on license suspended for DWI under § 46.2-391 (additional mandatory minimums)
notes: May also result in additional suspension period. If driving on DWI-suspended license, more severe penalties apply under § 18.2-272.

statute_title: Hit and Run — Failure to Stop at Accident
offense_class: Class 5 Felony (injury/death); Class 1 Misdemeanor (attended property damage); Class 4 Misdemeanor (unattended property)
penalty_max: 10 years (injury/death felony); 12 months (attended property); $250 fine (unattended property)
elements: Defendant was involved in a motor vehicle accident
Defendant failed to immediately stop at the scene
Defendant failed to provide identification, license, and registration
Defendant failed to render reasonable assistance to injured persons
enhancements: Accident resulting in injury or death (Class 5 Felony)
Accident resulting in death and defendant was DWI at the time (additional felony charges)
notes: Felony hit and run has no mandatory minimum but carries 1–10 years. Prosecution must prove defendant knew or should have known accident occurred.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed another person
The killing was willful, deliberate, and premeditated
Or the killing occurred during the commission of arson, rape, forcible sodomy, robbery, burglary, or abduction
enhancements: Aggravated murder under § 18.2-31 (life without parole)
Murder of law enforcement officer
Murder during commission of terrorism
notes: Virginia abolished the death penalty in 2021. Maximum sentence is life imprisonment. Aggravated murder under § 18.2-31 carries mandatory life without parole.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed another person
With malice aforethought
But without the willfulness, deliberation, and premeditation required for first degree murder
enhancements: Use of a firearm in the commission of murder (mandatory minimum 3 years under § 18.2-53.1)
notes: Second degree murder is all murder that is not aggravated or first degree. Implied malice (extreme recklessness showing disregard for human life) is sufficient.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed another person
The killing was intentional but occurred in the heat of passion
Upon reasonable provocation
notes: Class 5 Felony may be punished as a misdemeanor at jury/court discretion (up to 12 months jail and $2,500 fine). Distinguished from murder by absence of malice and presence of adequate provocation.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
The killing was unintentional
The killing resulted from criminal negligence or during the commission of an unlawful act not amounting to a felony
enhancements: DUI-related involuntary manslaughter under § 18.2-36.1 (mandatory 1 year for BAC 0.15+ or repeat DUI)
notes: Commonly charged in DUI-related fatalities as aggravated involuntary manslaughter under § 18.2-36.1 (Class 4 Felony, 1–10 years mandatory minimum).

elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated in violation of § 18.2-266
The intoxicated driving caused the death of another person
The defendant's conduct was so gross, wanton, and culpable as to show a reckless disregard for human life
mandatory_minimum: 1 year (mandatory minimum); 20 days mandatory if elevated BAC
enhancements: BAC 0.15 or higher at the time of the offense
Defendant had prior DUI convictions
notes: Supersedes general involuntary manslaughter when DUI is involved. Mandatory license revocation. Conviction cannot be suspended below mandatory minimum.

elements: Defendant committed an assault (attempted or threatened battery)
Or defendant committed a battery (unwanted touching done in a rude, angry, or vengeful manner)
Without legal justification
enhancements: Against law enforcement, firefighter, or EMS (6-month mandatory minimum under § 18.2-57(C))
Against teacher or school employee (mandatory 2 days jail under § 18.2-57(D))
Motivated by bias (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-57(B))
notes: Simple assault and battery is Virginia's most commonly charged violent misdemeanor. Assault (threat) and battery (contact) are distinct offenses but charged under the same statute.

elements: Defendant maliciously shot, stabbed, cut, or wounded another person
Or caused bodily injury by any means
With the intent to maim, disfigure, disable, or kill
enhancements: Permanent and significant physical impairment results (Class 2 Felony under § 18.2-51.2)
Against law enforcement officer (mandatory 2 years under § 18.2-51.1)
notes: Unlawful wounding under § 18.2-51 (without malice) is a Class 6 Felony (1–5 years). The distinction between malicious and unlawful wounding is the presence of malice.

statute_title: Shooting, Stabbing in Commission of Felony
elements: Defendant shot, stabbed, cut, or wounded another person
In the commission of or attempt to commit a felony
enhancements: If malice is proven, may be charged as malicious wounding (Class 3 Felony)
notes: Also applies to shooting at an occupied vehicle under § 18.2-154. Use of a firearm in commission of a felony carries mandatory 3 years under § 18.2-53.1.

statute_title: Assault and Battery Against Family or Household Member
offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first/second); Class 6 Felony (third within 20 years)
elements: Defendant committed an assault and battery
Against a family or household member as defined in § 16.1-228
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense within 20 years (Class 6 Felony)
Prior conviction for a violent felony against family member
Strangulation (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-51.6)
notes: Family or household members include spouses, former spouses, parents, children, and persons who cohabit or formerly cohabited. Protective orders available under § 16.1-279.1.

statute_title: Domestic Assault and Battery — Repeat Offense
offense_class: Class 6 Felony (third or subsequent within 20 years)
elements: Defendant committed assault and battery against a family or household member
Defendant has two or more prior convictions for assault against family members within the preceding 20 years
notes: Prior convictions from any jurisdiction count toward the 20-year lookback. Conviction triggers federal firearms disability under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9).

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first); Class 6 Felony (second within 5 years)
elements: Defendant engaged in conduct directed at another person on more than one occasion
The conduct placed or was intended to place the victim in reasonable fear of death, criminal sexual assault, or bodily injury
enhancements: Second or subsequent conviction within 5 years (Class 6 Felony)
Stalking in violation of a protective order (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Includes cyberstalking. Protective orders under § 19.2-152.10 available to victims.

offense_class: Class 5 Felony (abduction); Class 2 Felony (abduction with intent to extort or defile)
elements: Defendant seized, took, transported, detained, or secreted another person
By force, intimidation, or deception
With intent to deprive the person of personal liberty or withhold them from lawful authority
enhancements: Abduction with intent to defile or extort (Class 2 Felony under § 18.2-48)
Victim is a minor (enhanced penalties)
notes: Abduction under § 18.2-47 is the general statute. § 18.2-48 covers abduction with intent — much more severe. Parental abduction has separate provisions under § 18.2-49.1.

offense_class: Class 4 Felony (attempted second degree); Class 2 Felony (attempted first degree)
elements: Defendant took a direct but ineffectual act toward killing another person
With the specific intent to kill
enhancements: Use of a firearm (mandatory 3 years under § 18.2-53.1)
notes: Attempted aggravated murder is a Class 2 Felony with a possible sentence of 20 years to life.

elements: Defendant took property from the person or presence of another
By violence, threat, or intimidation
With intent to permanently deprive the owner of the property
enhancements: Use of a firearm (mandatory 3 years consecutive under § 18.2-53.1)
Causing serious bodily harm
notes: Virginia robbery statute does not distinguish degrees. All robbery carries 5 years to life. Carjacking is a separate offense under § 18.2-58.1 (15 years to life).

elements: Defendant committed robbery as defined in § 18.2-58
Defendant used or displayed a firearm during the commission of the robbery
mandatory_minimum: 3 years consecutive for firearm use under § 18.2-53.1, in addition to robbery sentence
enhancements: Second or subsequent firearm offense (mandatory 5 years consecutive under § 18.2-53.1)
notes: Virginia does not have a separate armed robbery statute. Armed robbery is charged as § 18.2-58 robbery plus the § 18.2-53.1 firearm mandatory minimum.

statute_title: Burglary — Nighttime, Dwelling, With Weapon or Assault
elements: Defendant broke and entered or entered and concealed himself in a dwelling
In the nighttime
With intent to commit a felony or larceny
While armed with a deadly weapon, or committed assault upon an occupant
notes: Virginia has multiple burglary statutes: § 18.2-89 (most serious — dwelling, nighttime, armed); § 18.2-90 (dwelling, nighttime, unarmed — Class 3 Felony); § 18.2-91 (dwelling, daytime or non-dwelling, nighttime — Class 2–6 Felony depending on circumstances).

statute_title: Entering Dwelling or Structure with Intent to Commit Crime
penalty_max: 5 years (felony); or 12 months (misdemeanor at court discretion)
elements: Defendant entered or broke and entered a dwelling or structure
In the daytime (dwelling) or nighttime (non-dwelling structure)
With intent to commit a larceny, assault, or other felony
enhancements: While armed with a deadly weapon (may elevate to Class 3 Felony under § 18.2-89 or § 18.2-90)
notes: Class 6 Felony can be treated as a misdemeanor at the discretion of the jury or court. Covers daytime dwelling entries and nighttime non-dwelling entries.

statute_title: Entering Structure Other Than Dwelling with Intent
elements: Defendant broke and entered or entered a non-dwelling structure
With intent to commit a felony, larceny, assault, or battery
notes: Commercial buildings, offices, and other structures not used as dwellings fall under this provision when entered during the day.

elements: Defendant took and carried away the property of another
Without the owner's consent
With intent to permanently deprive the owner of the property
The value of the property was $1,000 or more, or the property taken was a firearm regardless of value
enhancements: Larceny from the person (regardless of value, is grand larceny under § 18.2-95)
notes: Virginia raised the grand larceny threshold from $500 to $1,000 effective July 1, 2020. May be punished as a misdemeanor (up to 12 months and $2,500) at court discretion.

elements: Defendant took and carried away the property of another
Without the owner's consent
With intent to permanently deprive the owner
Value of property less than $1,000 (and not taken from the person)
enhancements: Third or subsequent petit larceny conviction (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-104)
notes: Shoplifting is covered under § 18.2-103 with same penalty structure. Third offense petit larceny becomes a felony.

elements: Defendant willfully concealed or took possession of merchandise offered for sale
With intent to convert the goods to defendant's own use without paying the purchase price
Or defendant altered the price tag of the merchandise
enhancements: Third or subsequent conviction (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-104)
Organized retail theft (enhanced penalties)
notes: Civil liability for shoplifting up to $350 in addition to criminal penalties. Store personnel have limited authority to detain suspected shoplifters under § 18.2-105.1.

elements: Defendant took, drove, or used a motor vehicle, aircraft, or boat
Without the consent of the owner
In the absence of the owner
With intent to temporarily deprive the owner of possession
enhancements: If intent is to permanently deprive, charged as grand larceny under § 18.2-95
notes: Unauthorized use (temporary) is a Class 6 Felony; theft (permanent deprivation) is grand larceny regardless of vehicle value.

elements: Defendant bought, received, or aided in concealing stolen goods
Defendant knew the goods were stolen
Intent to deprive the owner
notes: Penalty matches the underlying larceny offense. Grand larceny threshold ($1,000+) applies.

elements: Defendant obtained money, a signature, or other property
By any false pretense
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Value of $1,000 or more (felony, 1–20 years)
notes: Covers a wide range of fraud schemes. The $1,000 threshold mirrors the grand/petit larceny distinction.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first); Class 6 Felony (second+); Class 5 Felony (against minor or elder)
elements: Defendant obtained, recorded, or accessed identifying information of another person
Without the other person's consent
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Second or subsequent conviction (Class 6 Felony)
Victim is a minor or elderly person (Class 5 Felony)
Five or more victims in a single scheme (Class 5 Felony)
notes: Restitution to the victim is mandatory. Victims entitled to identity theft passport from Attorney General's office.

statute_title: Forging Public Records, Coins, or Bank Notes
elements: Defendant forged or counterfeited any coin, bank note, or public record
Or uttered or attempted to employ as true any forged instrument
Knowing the instrument to be false
notes: General forgery of other writings (checks, contracts) is a Class 5 Felony under § 18.2-172. Uttering (passing) a forged instrument is punished the same as the forgery.

elements: Defendant had lawful possession or control of money or property
By virtue of office, employment, or position of trust
Defendant wrongfully and fraudulently converted the property to personal use
enhancements: Value of $1,000 or more (felony)
notes: Threshold mirrors grand larceny. Embezzlement by public officers has enhanced penalties. Larceny by employee falls under this statute.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (under $1,000 in 6 months); Class 6 Felony ($1,000+ in 6 months)
elements: Defendant used a credit card or credit card number obtained or retained unlawfully
To obtain money, goods, or services
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Value obtained $1,000 or more within 6-month period (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Also covers credit card theft under § 18.2-192 and credit card forgery under § 18.2-193.

elements: Defendant made, drew, uttered, or delivered a check or draft
Defendant knew at the time there were insufficient funds in the account
With intent to defraud
notes: Prima facie evidence of intent to defraud if the check is dishonored and maker fails to pay within 5 days of written notice.

offense_class: Class 5 Felony (Schedule I/II); Class 1 Misdemeanor (Schedule III); Class 2 Misdemeanor (Schedule IV); Class 3 Misdemeanor (Schedule V/VI)
penalty_max: 10 years (Schedule I/II); 12 months (Schedule III); 6 months (Schedule IV)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed a controlled substance
The substance was listed in Schedules I through VI of the Drug Control Act
Defendant did not have a valid prescription
enhancements: Possession near a school (enhanced penalties under § 18.2-255.2)
notes: Virginia decriminalized simple marijuana possession. Schedule I/II possession (cocaine, heroin, meth, fentanyl) remains a Class 5 Felony but can be treated as a misdemeanor at court discretion.

offense_class: Civil violation (up to 1 oz); Class 1 Misdemeanor (over 1 oz, under 1 lb)
penalty_max: $25 civil penalty (up to 1 oz); 12 months (over 1 oz)
elements: Defendant possessed marijuana
Quantity exceeded personal possession limits or was in a prohibited location
enhancements: Possession of more than 1 oz (Class 1 Misdemeanor under § 4.1-1105.1)
Possession with intent to distribute (felony under § 18.2-248.1)
notes: Virginia legalized adult recreational marijuana possession up to 1 oz as of July 1, 2021. Retail sales not yet authorized. Public consumption remains illegal ($25 civil fine).

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed cocaine
Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Defendant did not have a valid prescription
enhancements: Possession near a school (enhanced penalties)
notes: Class 5 Felony may be punished as a misdemeanor (up to 12 months, $2,500 fine) at court discretion.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Defendant did not have a valid prescription
enhancements: Manufacturing methamphetamine (separate offense under § 18.2-248 with mandatory minimum)
notes: Methamphetamine manufacturing carries a mandatory 10–40 year sentence under federal sentencing guidelines. State charge may be reduced to misdemeanor at court discretion.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed a Schedule I or II opioid
Including heroin, fentanyl, or fentanyl analogs
Without a valid prescription
enhancements: Fentanyl-specific enhancements under § 18.2-248(H1) for distribution
notes: Fentanyl distribution causing death may be charged as felony homicide under § 18.2-33. Possession for personal use is Class 5 Felony but commonly reduced to misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
With intent to manufacture, sell, give, or distribute the substance
Knowledge of the nature and character of the substance
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (mandatory 5 years)
Distribution near a school (mandatory 1–5 years consecutive)
Distribution to a minor (mandatory 10–50 years)
notes: Intent to distribute may be inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, and other indicia. Schedule I/II first offense carries 5–40 years.

penalty_max: 40 years (Schedule I/II); Life (second offense Schedule I/II)
elements: Defendant manufactured, sold, gave, distributed, or possessed with intent to distribute a controlled substance
The substance was a Schedule I or II controlled substance
mandatory_minimum: 5 years (first offense, Schedule I/II); mandatory life (third offense)
enhancements: Second offense (5–life)
Third offense (mandatory life)
Distribution resulting in death
Distribution near school property (mandatory consecutive)
notes: Distribution of marijuana has separate penalties under § 18.2-248.1 — less than 1 oz is a Class 1 Misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant manufactured, sold, or distributed a controlled substance
In quantities meeting or exceeding trafficking thresholds (100g+ cocaine, 1kg+ marijuana)
enhancements: Importation into the Commonwealth (enhanced penalties)
Operating a continuing criminal enterprise
notes: Trafficking thresholds vary by substance. Cocaine: 100g+ (5-year mandatory min). Virginia also has the drug kingpin statute under § 18.2-248(H).

elements: Defendant manufactured or attempted to manufacture a controlled substance
Knowledge of the nature of the substance
enhancements: Manufacturing methamphetamine (20-year mandatory minimum under § 18.2-248(C))
Manufacturing near schools or daycares
notes: Methamphetamine manufacturing carries particularly severe penalties. Manufacturing includes all steps in the production process.

elements: Defendant possessed drug paraphernalia

With the intent to use it to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale, or otherwise introduce into the human body a controlled substance
enhancements: Sale or distribution of drug paraphernalia to a minor (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Marijuana paraphernalia exempted from criminal penalties following legalization. Sale of paraphernalia is a separate offense.

statute_title: Obtaining Drugs by Fraud or Forgery
elements: Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain a controlled substance
By fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, forgery, or subterfuge
Including use of a forged prescription
notes: Doctor shopping (visiting multiple providers for the same controlled substance) may be charged under this statute.

elements: Defendant carried about his person, hidden from common observation
A weapon such as a pistol, revolver, or other weapon designed or intended to propel a missile
Or any dirk, bowie knife, switchblade knife, razor, or similar weapon
Without a valid concealed handgun permit
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class 6 Felony)
Carrying in certain prohibited locations (schools, courthouses, places of worship)
notes: Virginia became a shall-issue state for concealed carry permits. Certain weapons (switchblades, ballistic knives) are prohibited regardless of permit status.

statute_title: Possession of Firearms by Convicted Felons
elements: Defendant possessed, transported, or carried a firearm
Defendant had been convicted of a felony
mandatory_minimum: 2 years (mandatory minimum if prior violent felony)
enhancements: Prior conviction for certain violent felonies (mandatory minimum 5 years under § 18.2-308.2(A))
notes: Also applies to persons involuntarily committed, subjects of protective orders, and certain drug offenders. Petition for restoration of rights available under § 18.2-308.2(C).

statute_title: Possession of Firearm on School Property
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
On the property of a public, private, or religious school
Or on a school bus
notes: Exceptions for law enforcement and authorized personnel. Concealed carry permit does not authorize carry on school grounds.

offense_class: Class 6 Felony (at occupied building); Class 1 Misdemeanor (within city limits)
elements: Defendant willfully discharged a firearm
Within or at an occupied building or in a populated area
In a manner that endangered the life or property of others
enhancements: Resulting in injury or death (additional felony charges)
notes: Shooting at an occupied building is a Class 4 Felony under § 18.2-279. Drive-by shooting is a separate offense under § 18.2-286.1.

elements: Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim
Against the victim's will by force, threat, or intimidation
Or the victim was mentally incapacitated or physically helpless
enhancements: Victim under 13 years old (mandatory life under § 18.2-61(A)(iii))
Defendant 18+ and victim under 13 (mandatory life)
notes: Virginia rape statute covers sexual intercourse accomplished through force, threat, intimidation, or victim incapacity. Marital rape is prosecutable.

elements: Defendant engaged in oral or anal sexual acts (cunnilingus, fellatio, anilingus, or anal intercourse)
Against the will of the victim by force, threat, or intimidation
Or the victim was mentally incapacitated or physically helpless
enhancements: Victim under 13 (mandatory life)
Use of force resulting in serious bodily injury
notes: Forcible sodomy is prosecuted with the same severity as rape. Object sexual penetration is covered under § 18.2-67.2.

elements: Defendant sexually abused the victim
Against the victim's will by force, threat, intimidation, or ruse
enhancements: Aggravated sexual battery (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-67.3 if victim under 13 or defendant uses force causing injury)
notes: Sexual battery is the misdemeanor-level sex offense in Virginia. Aggravated sexual battery is a felony with a 1–20 year range.

statute_title: Carnal Knowledge of a Minor (13–14 Years Old)
elements: Defendant had sexual intercourse with a person aged 13 or 14
Defendant was more than 3 years older than the victim
enhancements: Victim under 13 (charged as rape under § 18.2-61, mandatory life)
notes: Virginia's age of consent is 18. Consensual sex with a 15–17 year old by an adult is a Class 1 Misdemeanor (contributing to delinquency). The 3-year close-in-age exception applies.

statute_title: Sexual Abuse of a Child Under 15
elements: Defendant was 18 years of age or older
Defendant engaged in sexual contact with a child under 15
The act was done with lascivious intent
notes: Separate from sexual battery which requires force. This statute covers sexual contact with children based on age alone.

elements: Defendant knowingly possessed sexually explicit visual material
Depicting a minor
Defendant knew or should have known the subject was a minor
enhancements: Production or distribution of child pornography (Class 4 Felony, 5–20 years)
Second or subsequent offense (mandatory 1 year)
notes: Each image may constitute a separate offense. Manufacturing and distribution carry much more severe penalties.

statute_title: Failure to Register as Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender
Defendant knowingly failed to register or re-register as required
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Virginia Sex Offender Registry requirements under § 9.1-900 et seq.

elements: Defendant maliciously burned or destroyed by explosive
A dwelling house or manufactured home
Or any building adjoining or part of the curtilage of a dwelling
enhancements: Death resulting from arson (additional homicide charges)
Arson for insurance fraud
notes: Burning personal property to defraud an insurer is a separate offense under § 18.2-79. Arson of non-dwelling structures falls under § 18.2-80 (Class 4 Felony).

elements: Defendant unlawfully destroyed, defaced, damaged, or removed property
Of another person or entity
Without the owner's consent
enhancements: Damage to a house of worship, school, or community center (Class 6 Felony regardless of value)
notes: Restitution commonly ordered. The $1,000 felony threshold applies to the value of damage, not the value of the property.

statute_title: Destruction of Property — Graffiti and Defacement
elements: Defendant intentionally defaced, damaged, or destroyed public or private property
Including graffiti, tagging, or etching on surfaces
Without the owner's consent
enhancements: Defacement of a monument or memorial (enhanced to Class 6 Felony)
notes: Community service and restitution commonly ordered as conditions of probation.

elements: Defendant went or remained on the property of another
After having been forbidden to do so by the owner, lessee, or custodian
Or having been told to leave and failing to do so
notes: Includes going on land after having been forbidden to do so, either orally or by posted signs. Peeping Tom offense is a separate statute under § 18.2-130.

elements: Defendant was in a public place
Defendant engaged in conduct intending to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm
Or creating a risk thereof, by engaging in fighting, threatening, violent, or tumultuous behavior
notes: Includes intoxicated in public (§ 18.2-388 is a separate offense — Class 4 Misdemeanor, $250 fine).

statute_title: Profane Swearing and Intoxication in Public
elements: Defendant was intoxicated in public
Whether from alcohol, drugs, or other intoxicants
Defendant's behavior was disruptive or endangered self or others
notes: Class 4 Misdemeanor carries fine only, no jail time. May be charged in combination with disorderly conduct.

elements: Defendant intentionally made an obscene display of his or her person or private parts
In any public place or in a place where others were present
enhancements: Third or subsequent conviction (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Indecent exposure involving a victim under 13 may be charged under more serious sex offense statutes.

elements: Defendant used a computer or computer network to communicate
Obscene, vulgar, profane, lewd, lascivious, or indecent language or threats
To coerce, intimidate, or harass any person
enhancements: Threat to kill communicated by computer (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Virginia also has a telephone harassment statute under § 18.2-429. General threats statute is § 18.2-60.

statute_title: Threat to Kill or Do Bodily Injury
offense_class: Class 6 Felony (threat to kill); Class 1 Misdemeanor (threat of bodily harm)
penalty_max: 5 years (felony threat to kill); 12 months (misdemeanor threat)
elements: Defendant knowingly communicated a threat
To kill or do bodily injury to a person or family member
The threat placed the victim in reasonable apprehension of death or bodily injury
enhancements: Threat communicated in writing (Class 6 Felony regardless of content)
Threat to employees of schools (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Written threats are automatically Class 6 Felonies. Oral threats of bodily harm are Class 1 Misdemeanors.

elements: Defendant knowingly attempted to prevent a law enforcement officer from performing official duties
By physical force, threat, intimidation, or physical obstruction
enhancements: Use of threats or force that puts officer at risk of death or serious bodily injury (Class 6 Felony under § 18.2-460(C))
notes: Passive non-cooperation (going limp) versus active resistance (pulling away, fleeing) may affect the charge level.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (without force); Class 6 Felony (with force or threats)
elements: Defendant without just cause knowingly obstructed any law enforcement officer
In the performance of duties
Or failed to cease an illegal act upon being advised to stop
enhancements: Obstruction involving threats of bodily harm to officer (Class 6 Felony)
notes: May be charged in addition to the underlying offense. Covers interference with judicial proceedings, police investigations, and court orders.

offense_class: Class 2 Misdemeanor (general); Class 6 Felony (endangerment or speed 20+ over limit)
elements: A law enforcement officer signaled or directed the defendant to stop
Defendant willfully disregarded the signal
Defendant fled or attempted to elude the officer
enhancements: Speed 20+ mph over limit during pursuit (Class 6 Felony)
Eluding resulting in death of another (Class 4 Felony)
notes: Separate from resisting arrest. Felony eluding requires endangerment of persons or property during the pursuit.

penalty_max: 10 days jail and/or $250 fine (summary); indefinite for civil contempt
elements: Defendant committed an act of misbehavior in the presence of the court
Or willfully disobeyed a lawful order, process, or command of the court
notes: Civil contempt (coercive) ends when the defendant complies. Criminal contempt (punitive) has a fixed sentence. Separate from violation of protective order.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (first); Class 6 Felony (third within 20 years or with assault)
elements: A protective order was in effect against the defendant
Defendant violated a provision of the protective order
Defendant had knowledge of the order
enhancements: Third or subsequent violation within 20 years (Class 6 Felony)
Violation involving assault and battery (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Includes emergency, preliminary, and permanent protective orders. GPS monitoring may be ordered for repeat violators.

statute_title: Violation of Conditions of Suspension of Sentence or Probation
offense_class: May be resentenced to any punishment that could have been originally imposed
penalty_max: Up to the maximum of the original suspended sentence
elements: Defendant was placed on probation or received a suspended sentence
Defendant violated one or more conditions of probation
The violation was proven by a preponderance of the evidence
notes: Court must consider graduated sanctions before revocation under recent Virginia reforms. Technical violations distinguished from new criminal conduct.

penalty_max: 14 days (first technical violation); 14 days per subsequent
elements: Defendant committed a technical violation of probation
Not involving a new criminal offense
notes: Virginia limits incarceration for technical probation violations. Graduated sanctions must be used before revocation.

statute_title: Substantive Violation of Probation — New Criminal Conduct
penalty_max: Up to the maximum of the original suspended sentence
elements: Defendant was on probation or had a suspended sentence
Defendant committed a new criminal offense while on probation
notes: New criminal conduct allows full revocation without graduated sanctions limitation. Original sentence may be imposed in full.

offense_class: Class 1 Misdemeanor (misdemeanor charge); Class 6 Felony (felony charge)
elements: Defendant was on bail or recognizance
Defendant was given notice of the court date
Defendant willfully failed to appear as required
notes: FTA triggers a capias (arrest warrant) and potential bail revocation. Bail bondsman may also have the bond forfeited.

statute_title: Making a False Report to Law Enforcement
elements: Defendant knowingly gave a false report
To any law enforcement official
Of the commission of a crime
notes: Includes false reports of bomb threats (Class 5 Felony under § 18.2-83) and false emergency calls.

offense_class: Class 4 Felony (serious injury); Class 6 Felony (willful act causing injury)
elements: Defendant was a parent, guardian, or person responsible for a child
Defendant willfully acted in a manner that was so gross, wanton, and culpable as to show reckless disregard for human life
Resulting in serious injury to the child
enhancements: Death of the child (murder or manslaughter charges)
notes: Failure to provide necessities (food, shelter, medical care) may also be charged under this statute. Mandatory reporting obligations under § 63.2-1509.

statute_title: Child Endangerment — Willful Act or Omission
elements: Defendant was responsible for the care of a child under 18
Defendant's willful act or omission
Caused or permitted serious injury to the life or health of the child
notes: May be charged alongside DUI when a minor is in the vehicle.

statute_title: Abuse and Neglect of Incapacitated Adults
offense_class: Class 4 Felony (serious injury); Class 6 Felony (general abuse)
elements: Defendant was responsible for the care of an incapacitated adult
Defendant abused, neglected, or exploited the incapacitated adult
Resulting in injury or financial loss
enhancements: Death resulting from abuse (additional homicide charges)
notes: Includes financial exploitation. Adult Protective Services must be notified. Mandatory reporting under § 63.2-1606.

statute_title: Insurance Fraud — False Statement to Obtain Payment
elements: Defendant presented a false or misleading statement or claim
To an insurance company
With intent to defraud the insurer
notes: Separate from general obtaining money by false pretenses. Arson to defraud insurance is covered under § 18.2-79.

offense_class: Class 5 Felony (conspiracy to commit non-capital felony); Class 3 Felony (conspiracy to commit capital or Class 1/2 Felony)
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit a felony
An overt act was taken in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: Conspiracy to distribute drugs (penalties match the underlying drug offense)
notes: Conspiracy to commit a misdemeanor is a Class 3 Misdemeanor. Withdrawal from conspiracy is a defense if communicated to co-conspirators and all overt acts cease.

elements: Defendant offered money or its equivalent
For sexual acts (including intercourse, cunnilingus, fellatio, anilingus, anal intercourse, or animate or inanimate object sexual penetration)
And any act in furtherance was committed
enhancements: Solicitation of a minor (Class 6 Felony)
notes: Virginia revised its prostitution statutes effective 2021 to decriminalize selling sex while maintaining criminality of buying sex.

elements: Defendant remained in a public place
Without apparent purpose
After being asked to leave by a law enforcement officer or property owner
notes: Often charged as part of the disorderly conduct statute. Some local loitering ordinances may apply additionally.

statute_title: Drinking or Possessing Open Container in Motor Vehicle
offense_class: Traffic infraction; Class 4 Misdemeanor (in certain circumstances)
elements: Defendant was a passenger or driver of a motor vehicle
On a public highway
Defendant possessed an open container of alcohol while the vehicle was in operation
notes: Virginia prohibits open containers of alcohol in the passenger area of a motor vehicle on public highways.

fine_max: $500,000 or twice the value laundered (whichever is greater)
elements: Defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
Knowing the property involved was the proceeds of criminal activity
With intent to promote the carrying on of the criminal activity or to conceal the nature, location, source, ownership, or control of the proceeds
notes: Virginia's money laundering statute parallels the federal statute. $10,000+ transactions trigger additional reporting requirements.

elements: Defendant used a computer or computer network without authority
To obtain property or services by false pretenses
Or to convert the property of another
enhancements: Value of $2,500 or more (Class 5 Felony)
notes: Virginia's Computer Crimes Act (§ 18.2-152.1 et seq.) covers wire-type fraud. Federal wire fraud charges under 18 U.S.C. § 1343 may also apply.

elements: Defendant employed a device, scheme, or artifice to defraud
In connection with the offer, sale, or purchase of a security
Or made untrue statements of material fact or omitted material facts
notes: Virginia's Securities Act provides for both criminal prosecution and civil remedies. State Corporation Commission has enforcement authority.

offense_class: Affirmative defense — not a separate charge
elements: Defendant reasonably believed that force was necessary
To protect against imminent unlawful use of force by another
Defendant used no more force than was reasonably necessary under the circumstances
Defendant was not the initial aggressor (or had effectively withdrawn)
notes: Virginia does not have a statutory stand-your-ground law but follows castle doctrine for defense of the home. Duty to retreat applies in some circumstances outside the home.

elements: Elements vary by specific offense
notes: Catch-all category for Virginia offenses not individually listed. Includes: hunting violations, ABC violations, environmental crimes, traffic infractions, and other regulatory offenses.
